title: RBI Sells Dollars in Offshore and Onshore Markets as Rupee Nears Record Low Amid Oil Surge
excerpt: India's central bank stepped in after the rupee fell to 96.45 per dollar, its weakest since May, as Brent crude breached $90 on escalating US-Iran tensions.
body:
• The RBI sold US dollars in both offshore and onshore markets to arrest the rupee's slide toward its record low of 96.96 per dollar.
  • Brent crude has surged over 20% in two weeks, crossing $90 per barrel as the US-Iran conflict chokes the Strait of Hormuz.
  • India's FCNR deposit drive has attracted only $10 billion of an expected $30–60 billion, falling short of market expectations.
  • The benchmark 10-year government bond yield climbed 4 basis points to 6.82%, signaling broader financial market stress.

The Reserve Bank of India intervened in foreign exchange markets on Monday, selling US dollars in both offshore and onshore markets after the rupee weakened sharply toward its record low, according to traders familiar with the matter.

The rupee fell as much as 0.2% to 96.4575 per dollar during the session, putting it within striking distance of the all-time low of 96.9650 touched in late May. The currency eventually closed at 96.4450, limiting losses after the central bank's intervention through state-run banks.

Oil Prices Drive the Pressure

The rupee's decline was driven primarily by a renewed surge in global crude oil prices. Brent crude breached $90 per barrel on Monday — a jump of more than 20% over the past two weeks — as escalating hostilities between the United States and Iran raised concerns over supply disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz.

"USD/INR continues to face upward pressure amid higher oil prices and increased importer USD buying."

— Barclays Bank strategists, including Mitul Kotecha

Crude oil accounts for more than two-thirds of India's import bill. Higher prices increase demand for US dollars from importers, putting direct pressure on the rupee and straining the country's foreign exchange reserves.

FCNR Measures Fall Short

Authorities have taken steps to shore up the currency. On June 5, the RBI unveiled measures to attract more foreign currency by easing rules for bond investments and encouraging dollar deposits from non-resident Indians through a special FCNR swap facility.

The measures initially worked — the rupee strengthened to as much as 94.14 in late June. But the rally has since evaporated as higher oil prices revived demand for the greenback. India has attracted roughly $10 billion under the deposit programme so far, according to Reuters, well below the $30–60 billion that economists and bankers had estimated the programme could generate by its September 30 deadline.

What NRIs Should Watch

For non-resident Indians, the rupee's weakness presents a mixed picture. Remittances now stretch further in rupee terms, and the FCNR deposit scheme offers attractive returns on dollar savings. But the underlying cause — surging oil prices from the US-Iran conflict — threatens India's growth-inflation balance and could prompt the RBI to raise interest rates.

Swap markets are currently pricing about 70 basis points of rate hikes by the RBI over the next 12 months. Traders expect the rupee to remain highly sensitive to oil prices, with fresh all-time lows possible if Brent crosses $95 per barrel.

"If Brent crude prices continue to keep rising and cross $95 per barrel, the rupee would be prone to fresh all-time lows," a foreign exchange salesperson at a foreign bank told Reuters.

Looking Ahead

The focus this week shifts to foreign portfolio flows and any diplomatic developments in the Middle East that could ease oil prices. Overseas investors have net bought $2.3 billion of Indian stocks and bonds so far in July. But with the US having completed nine consecutive nights of strikes against Iran, risks remain skewed to the upside for both volatility and the dollar.
